title: Pauri 40, sound: anad sunahu
hook: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace gives the Word, and your line, grace gives. Did you take one gift without evening the account? Today is day four hundred on this path. Thank you for walking it. And today, the last pauri of the Anand. Day four hundred.

Some songs end by turning to face the room. The singer stops singing about something and starts singing to the people in front of her. Anand Sahib does that in its last pauri. After thirty-nine stanzas, the fortieth opens with a call: two short words and then a long one, the way you'd call across a crowded hall to get everyone's attention. You've already learned the sound of the Anand's first pauri. Today, the sound of the fortieth, the one that closes the whole song of bliss. Today: pauri forty, the sound.
screen: `A SONG TURNS TO FACE THE ROOM.` → `THE LAST PAURI OPENS WITH A CALL.` → `TODAY: THE SOUND OF THE FORTIETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, slowly: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore. Take it in pieces. Anad: a-NUD. Notice it's not quite anand, the word in the title of the whole song. The Gurmukhi here is written without the nasal sound, anad, a short, open word. Then sunahu: su-NA-hu, three soft syllables, and it's a call: hear. Then the long one: vaddabhaageeho. Vadd, with the tongue curled back a little for the d, then bhaa, then gee, then ho: vadd-BHAA-gee-ho. It's a word for a group of people, said as if calling across a room. Then sagal: sa-GAL, all. Manorath: ma-NO-rath. And poore: POO-re, two beats, the last one light. Put it together: anad sunahu, vaddabhaageeho, sagal manorath poore. Hear how it moves. Two short words like a knock on the door, a long word that opens it, and then a line that lands. Many ragis sing it to a tune that lifts on vaddabhaageeho and settles on poore. The pauri goes on for five more lines and ends, the way Guru Amar Das ends so many, with the name Nanak and a sound of its own: the unstruck music playing. That's tomorrow. For today, let the first line get into your mouth. And this is the pauri the sangat sings after the first five at the close of services, so it's a line many Sikhs have sung hundreds of times. Anad sunahu.
screen: `ANAD: A-NUD, NOT QUITE ANAND.` · `SUNAHU: SU-NA-HU, A CALL.` · `VADDABHAAGEEHO: VADD-BHAA-GEE-HO.` · `SAGAL MANORATH POORE: A LINE THAT LANDS.` · then, large: `ANAD SUNAHU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Not perfectly, just aloud. Anad sunahu. Pause. Vaddabhaageeho. Pause. Sagal manorath poore. Say it again, a little slower, and listen to your own voice the way you'd listen to someone else's. If you know the tune, you can hum it. Then let the line go and rest in the quiet it leaves behind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once at the end. The bell holds the time.
Pauri forty. The last pauri of the Anand, sung with the first five at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies. It begins: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore.
Your line: anad sunahu. Today, say it once under your breath at some point you'd normally rush past, a doorway, a red light. Day four hundred.

howItsDone: At the close of most Sikh services and ceremonies, the sangat sings six pauris of the Anand, the first five and the fortieth, before Ardas; many Sikhs also recite all forty pauris as part of their morning prayers.

they are the first five and the fortieth, the last.
in pauri forty the opening word is written anad, without the nasal
pauri forty ends with the name Nanak
like so many of Guru Amar Das's pauris.

fork.setup: the program is ending and the ragis start the six pauris of the Anand. which six are they?
options: pauris one to five, and pauri forty.
fork.reveal: the first five and the very last; together they are sung to close services and ceremonies, and the fortieth is today's.

original.note: Gurmukhi: anad sunahu, the opening words of the fortieth and last pauri of the Anand.

trapdoor: what you thought: anad is just a typo for anand.
what it means: it's how the word is written and sung in this pauri, a-NUD, opening the Anand's final pauri.
what a scholar hears: gurbani spelling preserves forms like anad beside anand, and the vowel signs at word ends often mark grammar, so reciters keep the written form exactly.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on the six pauris of Anand at the close of services

notes: Transliteration and syllable breaks for pauri 40's first line (anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore): confirm, especially that the Gurmukhi reads ਅਨਦੁ (without tippi) in this pauri.
'Many ragis sing it to a tune that lifts on vaddabhaageeho and settles on poore': a general description; tunes vary. Confirm or soften.
The trapdoor's note that word-final vowel signs often mark grammar (e.g. the aunkar on ਅਨਦੁ): confirm phrasing.
